title: Two and a Half Letters
hook: a weaver's two-line answer to a shelf of books
carry: bhakti: love, not books, makes the pandit
tomorrow: Why does a deer search the forest for a scent it carries?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's first doha. I went looking for the bad one, found no one, then searched my own heart.

A shelf sags under the weight of books, commentaries on commentaries. A scholar has spent his life there, and he can quote line and verse on anything you ask. Down the lane, a weaver throws the shuttle back and forth at his loom. Tradition says he never learned to read. He has a two-line answer for the man with the shelf, about how much reading it takes to become wise. His count is very small.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `A WEAVER AT HIS LOOM.` → `A VERY SMALL COUNT.`

segments.voice: Today's doha begins, in Hindi, pothi padh padh jag mua. A pothi is a book, a sacred text, and the line says, roughly: reading book after book, the whole world died, and not one became a pandit, a truly learned one. Then the second line: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Two and a half letters is the doha's own count, and one common reading makes it a joke you can see on the page. The Hindi word for love, prem, is written with a half letter joined to the front of a full one, and then one more. Kabir doesn't say books are bad; his own verses ended up in books. He says something narrower and sharper: reading alone doesn't finish anyone. This is the heart of bhakti, the path of devotion all this week's saints walked. In their teaching, God is reached by prem, love, and love can't be finished on paper. A grandmother who sings to Ram with her whole heart may have read more of it than the man with the shelf. And here's the trap, like yesterday's. Some readers stop at the first line, pleased: ha, all those books. But the second line asks something of them too. Have you read the two and a half letters? Not heard of them. Read them. In Kabir's picture, love of God is the text, every day is the exam, and the exam isn't on paper.
screen: `READING BOOK AFTER BOOK.` · `NOT ONE BECAME A PANDIT.` · `TWO AND A HALF LETTERS.` · then, large: `BHAKTI: WHOEVER READS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one name of God you love: Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, or the one your family uses. Say or sing it slowly three times, not as a lesson, but the way you'd say the name of someone you love. That's the bhakti way of reading the two and a half letters. If you don't pray, say the name of someone you love the same way, and notice what changes in your voice.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: reading book after book, no one became wise; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.
Your line: bhakti: love, not books, makes the pandit. Two and a half letters, prem, and a lifetime to read them. Day nine hundred twenty-two, done.

screen: `DAY 922 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES A DEER SEARCH THE FOREST FOR A SCENT IT CARRIES?`

howItsDone: This doha of Kabir is quoted in Hindi homes and classrooms as a saying about love and learning, and is sung in devotional settings by those who keep Kabir's songs.

pandit.meaning: a truly learned one, a wise scholar

doha.meaning: a couplet: two rhyming lines, easy to remember

Kabir.meaning: the weaver-poet of Kashi, famous for his dohas

bhakti.meaning: devotion; the path of loving God
